chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE)

questions.question: Why did organising the early Plebeian Council by curiae help the patricians?
options: Votes were counted by patrician priests
Only landowners were allowed to join a curia
Curiae could meet only when the consuls allowed
Patricians held half the seats in every curia
Many plebeians voted as their patrician patrons wished
questions.explanation: In the curiae, many plebeians depended on patrician patrons and voted as instructed. This let aristocrats quietly steer who became tribune.
questions.sourceQuote: The assembly was first organised by curiae, ancient groupings of families in which many plebeians depended on patrician patrons and voted as those patrons wished.

questions.question: During the second secession, where did the people gather before withdrawing to the Sacred Mount?
options: The Janiculum
The Palatine
The Capitoline
The Quirinal
The Aventine
questions.explanation: The people first gathered on the Aventine hill, then withdrew to the Sacred Mount. The anger had spread from the crowd to the army camped outside the city.
questions.sourceQuote: The people gathered on the Aventine, one of Rome's hills, then withdrew to the Sacred Mount.

questions.question: Why was a secession such a powerful weapon for the plebeians?
options: They could call on foreign allies for help
They were most Romans and produced most food and goods
They controlled the city's temples and treasury
They held most of the seats in the Senate
They owned all of the city's grain warehouses
questions.explanation: The plebs were the vast majority and produced most of Rome's food and goods. When they left, trade stopped and the city faced its enemies with no army.
questions.sourceQuote: Plebeians were the vast majority of Romans and produced most of the city's food and goods.

questions.question: In 462 BC, what did a tribune claim about the consuls?
options: They had stolen from the city's treasury
They were plotting to bring back the kings
They had betrayed Rome to the Volsci
They were too weak to defend the city
They had become more oppressive than the kings
questions.explanation: The tribune said the consuls were worse than the kings they had replaced. He proposed a commission to define and limit their powers.
questions.sourceQuote: In 462 BC a tribune declared that the consuls had become more oppressive than the kings they replaced, and proposed a commission to define and limit their powers.

questions.question: Tribunes commanded no troops. How could a tribune protect a citizen from a magistrate?
options: By placing his own untouchable person in the way
By bribing the magistrate's guards
By calling out a plebeian militia
By appealing to the gods in a temple
By paying the citizen's fine himself
questions.explanation: Because tribunes were sacrosanct, a tribune could physically stand between a citizen and a magistrate. From this grew the power of veto.
questions.sourceQuote: Shielded by this, a tribune could protect a citizen from a magistrate by placing his own untouchable person in the way.

questions.question: How did one hard-line consul respond to the public outcry over debt in 495 BC?
options: He reinforced creditors' right to imprison debtors
He created the office of tribune of the plebs
He exiled the city's leading moneylenders
He cancelled all debts owed to patricians
He gave public land to ruined veterans
questions.explanation: Instead of relief, the consul strengthened creditors' power to imprison debtors. The next year the plebeian soldiers refused to march.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead, one hard-line consul issued decrees reinforcing creditors' right to imprison debtors.

questions.question: In the early Republic, who alone could stand for office?
options: Wealthy plebeian traders
Any citizen-soldier
Only the pontiffs
Former army officers
The patricians
questions.explanation: Only the patricians, a small circle of aristocratic families, could stand for office. Both the consuls and the Senate came from their ranks.
questions.sourceQuote: Both belonged to the patricians, a small circle of aristocratic families who alone could stand for office.

questions.question: Why do historians find the lack of bloodshed in the early conflict odd?
options: Ancient sources describe constant street battles
The patricians had hired foreign mercenaries
The plebeians controlled all of the army's weapons
Roman law demanded death for any rebellion
Similar quarrels in the late Republic quickly turned violent
questions.explanation: Such bitter grievances produced surprisingly little violence, unlike the late Republic's quarrels. This is one of several puzzles that make the traditional story controversial.
questions.sourceQuote: It is odd that such bitter grievances led to so little bloodshed, when similar quarrels in the late Republic quickly turned violent.

questions.question: Why did the Senate choose Menenius Agrippa as its negotiator in 494 BC?
options: He commanded the army facing the Volsci
He had written down Rome's first laws
He was a former consul well liked by ordinary Romans
He was the chief priest of Rome
He had led the plebeian walkout himself
questions.explanation: The Senate needed someone the strikers would trust, so it chose a popular former consul. Tradition says he persuaded them with the fable of the belly.
questions.sourceQuote: It chose Menenius Agrippa, a former consul who was well liked by ordinary Romans.

questions.question: Why was military service a trap for plebeian soldiers in the early Republic?
options: They had to pay for their own warships
They lost their vote while they were enlisted
Their farms lay abandoned while they were on campaign
They were sent abroad for decades at a time
They were paid only in conquered land
questions.explanation: While soldiers were away, their farms went untended. Many had to borrow from patricians, and defaulting debtors could be beaten, imprisoned or even enslaved.
questions.sourceQuote: While a plebeian soldier was away on campaign, his farm lay abandoned.
